description: Ми — команда студентів-початківців, які цікавляться космосом, технологіями та дослідженням Всесвіту. Участь у хакатоні NASA для нас — це можливість отримати новий досвід, спробувати свої сили в командній роботі та дізнатися більше про космічні місії. У нашому проєкті ми хочемо розповісти про покинуті космічні апарати та роботизовані місії NASA, які залишили свій слід у дослідженні космосу.
summary:
Silent Explorers is an interactive website where NASA spacecraft left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space tell their own stories in first person. It is made for kids aged 10–14 and anyone curious about space.

Users pick a world and explore a map showing where 17 spacecraft rest today, from the Apollo 11 lunar module and Surveyor 3 to Opportunity, Ingenuity, Dawn and Pioneer 10. When a spacecraft is selected and the user scrolls down, its story comes alive: the spacecraft turns, the years of its mission count up, and fun facts, a mission timeline and a quick quiz appear one by one. Every story links to its NASA source.

Most people only hear about active missions, while older ones are described in dry technical tables. Our site turns real NASA data into short, memorable stories, so young people learn what these machines discovered and feel connected to the history of space exploration. The site works in Ukrainian and English, on desktop and mobile.
details:
What it does
Silent Explorers is a website where NASA hardware left on the Moon, on Mars and in deep space tells its own story. The user picks one of three worlds (Moon, Mars, deep space) and sees a map with 17 spacecraft placed where they rest today: the Apollo 11 descent stage, the Apollo 15 Lunar Roving Vehicle, the Apollo 12 ALSEP station, Surveyor 3, Viking 1 and 2, Sojourner, Spirit, Opportunity, Phoenix, InSight, Ingenuity, Dawn, NEAR Shoemaker, Kepler, Pioneer 10 and Pioneer 11.

How it works
Clicking a marker opens a short summary. When the user scrolls down, a story scene starts: the spacecraft rotates over its planet, a dust trail follows it, and a large counter runs through the years of the mission (for Opportunity, from 2004 to 2018). Chapters appear one by one: a first-person story, fun facts, a mission timeline and a quiz question. Visited spacecraft turn green on the map, and a progress bar shows how many of the 17 explorers the user has met. Each story links to its NASA source page. The site has Ukrainian and English versions and works on desktop and mobile.

Benefits and impact
Most students only hear about active missions, while older ones are described in technical catalogs that are hard for kids to read. We turn real mission data into short stories told by the spacecraft itself, which makes the science easier to remember and helps students see how today's missions grew out of earlier ones. Teachers can use it in class as a ready-made interactive lesson. In the future we want to add more spacecraft, more languages and lesson plans for teachers.

Tools and technologies
HTML, CSS and JavaScript in a single file, with no frameworks or server. Maps and illustrations are drawn in code (SVG and CSS), and the background rockets come from our earlier project, COSMOS. The site is hosted on GitHub Pages. We used an AI assistant to help write code and draft texts; the team chose the concept and the spacecraft and checked every fact against NASA sources.

Creativity
Instead of a list of facts, every spacecraft speaks for itself, and the scroll animation makes reading feel like a short film. The quiz and the collect-them-all progress turn learning into a game.

What we considered
Accuracy: dates, landing sites and status come from NASA NSSDCA and science.nasa.gov. Age: short texts and simple words for 10–14 year olds. Accessibility: keyboard navigation, readable contrast, animations turn off for users who prefer reduced motion, and the site works on phones.
dataRefs: NASA Space Science Data Coordinated Archive (NSSDCA)
